analysis.one_liner: Lets 50-to-64-year-olds buy into Medicare and lifts the ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices.
analysis.headline: The Medicare at 50 Act never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let anyone aged 50 to 64 buy into Medicare and receive the same hospital, doctor, and prescription drug benefits as people 65 and older, with help paying premiums modeled on the Affordable Care Act's subsidies. It also would have repealed the law that forbids Medicare from negotiating prescription drug prices. It was introduced by Senator Stabenow with 19 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: People aged 50 to 64 who are uninsured, have unaffordable private coverage, or lose employer coverage late in their careers would gain access to Medicare's provider network and benefits, with premium and cost-sharing help equal to what they would have received on an ACA exchange. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers generally would also benefit from the repeal of the ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices.

how_it_helps.text: Every citizen or permanent resident aged 50 to 64 would be eligible to enroll in Medicare and receive the same Part A, B, and D benefits and protections as people 65 and older, including access to Medicare Advantage plans and the Medicare Beneficiary Ombudsman.

Enrollees would receive financial assistance substantially similar to ACA exchange premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, with the bill directing particular attention to people with incomes below 200 percent of poverty.

The bill repeals the 'non-interference' provisions that prohibit the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services from negotiating prescription drug prices or establishing a formulary under the Medicare drug benefit.

Enrollees would get guaranteed-issue rights for Medigap supplemental policies on first enrollment and each re-enrollment, and states and nonprofits would receive $500 million a year in grants for outreach and enrollment help.

analysis.who_pays: Enrollees would pay premiums set to cover Medicare's estimated average per-person cost (plus any extra for pricier Medicare Advantage or drug plans), and taxpayers would fund the $500 million annual outreach grants. Prescription drug manufacturers would bear reduced revenue if Medicare used its new negotiation authority, and private insurers would lose some of the 50-to-64 individual market to a cheaper public option.

drawbacks.text: Premiums are set at Medicare's estimated full average per-person cost, not a discounted public rate, and the subsidy help is capped at ACA-exchange levels, so coverage could still be unaffordable for many people in the 50-to-64 age group.

The bill explicitly prohibits states from buying their Medicaid beneficiaries aged 50 to 64 into Medicare and bars people eligible for Medicaid from getting coverage through this route, so the poorest in the age group would not benefit.
The bill requires the Secretary to implement it with no negative impact on the existing Medicare trust funds, a constraint that limits how far premiums or subsidies could be enriched.

A buy-in open to 50-to-64-year-olds could draw some enrollees out of ACA exchange plans and employer-style individual coverage; a standard concern with buy-in proposals is that the mix of people who switch could raise premiums for those left in the private market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage expansion is real and targeted at a group — late-career adults — with some of the highest uninsured and premium costs in the country, and the drug-price negotiation repeal is a separate, significant win for taxpayers and Medicare beneficiaries. The main design limits are that premiums are actuarially full-cost, Medicaid beneficiaries are locked out, and the subsidies only match what the ACA already offers. Critics of Medicare negotiation authority argue reduced drug revenue could slow new drug development; the bill's backers would answer that the negotiation ban has kept Medicare paying some of the highest drug prices in the world.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2021, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Stabenow introduced the bill on April 21, 2021 with 18 initial cosponsors listed in the bill text, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The full action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call at any point; the referral to Finance was the last action of record.
The bill attracted 19 cosponsors in total, all Democrats, out of 48 Senate Democrats, and no Republican signed on.
A companion House approach — a Medicare buy-in starting at 60 — was part of broader Democratic health care proposals in this period, but this Senate bill never advanced alongside them.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers kept the legal ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices, and private insurers kept the 50-to-64 individual and exchange market to themselves; Americans in that age group without affordable coverage gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare at 50 Act and lined up Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 19 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote — in the two-plus years remaining in the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it sat in committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; because the bill never reached a vote, there is no roll call to show how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill repeals the statutory ban on Medicare negotiating drug prices and setting a formulary, directly threatening the industry's guaranteed high Medicare prices. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers pay those prices today, so the industry's interest ran against the public's on this provision.

A Medicare buy-in would pull many 50-to-64-year-olds out of individually purchased private insurance, but insurers could still serve enrollees through Medicare Advantage plans, which the bill explicitly preserves. The bill requires the Secretary to consult with insurance companies and other interested parties when writing regulations.

The bill extends guaranteed-issue rights for Medigap policies to buy-in enrollees at age 50 rather than 65, opening a new customer base — while also protecting them from being denied or priced based on health status.
